# The Tyranny of the Next Thing

There is a peculiar quality to modern life that I find endlessly fascinating: we have become almost pathologically incapable of staying with a single moment. We treat our own attention like an endless resource to be spent on everything and committed to nothing. We scroll, we skim, we half-listen, we half-read, and we call this "being connected." But connection to what, exactly?

I think about this a lot.

Consider the ordinary experience of eating a meal. In some cultures, the preparation of food is itself a meditative act. The careful cutting of vegetables. The patient stirring of a pot. The way steam rises and curls in the kitchen light. Eating, too, is deliberate — flavors are noticed, textures are savored, the simple act of nourishing one's body becomes a conversation between self and world. This is not romanticism. This is simply what happens when attention is directed rather than scattered.

Now consider how many of us actually eat. We eat over laptops. We eat while scrolling phones. We eat in our cars on the way somewhere else. The food passes from hand to mouth and we taste almost nothing of it. We are not eating — we are refueling a machine, and the machine is only marginally aware that the refueling is happening.

This seems like a small thing. It is not. It is, in miniature, the story of an entire way of being.

The ancient Greeks had a word — *ponos* — that referred to the kind of hard work that transforms you. Not busywork. Not the frantic productivity of an inbox at zero. Real labor. The kind that shapes your character the way water shapes stone. The distinction matters enormously. Because much of what we call "work" and "activity" is actually just motion without meaning. We are doing, doing, doing, but we are not being changed by it. We are not sharpening ourselves against any meaningful resistance.

There is a concept in the philosophy of mind called "deep attention" — the ability to focus intensely on a single thing for a sustained period. The neuroscientist Maryanne Wolf has written beautifully about this, about how deep reading, for instance, actually rewires the brain in ways that skimming never can. When you read a novel slowly, when you let the sentences accumulate, when you allow yourself to feel the rhythm of the prose and the weight of the ideas — you are not just processing information. You are building a self.

This is the part that fascinates me. Attention is not passive. Attention is creative. What you pay attention to, and how you pay attention to it, literally constitutes who you become. The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that "attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity." I think she was right, but I would go further: attention is also the purest form of self-creation. You are, in the deepest sense, what you notice.

And so the great question of a life is not really "What should I do?" It is "What deserves my attention?" This reframes everything. Suddenly, the question of career becomes a question about what kind of thinking you want to sustain across decades. The question of relationships becomes a question about who is worth the slow, difficult, undivided gaze of your notice. The question of leisure becomes a question about what kind of experience will leave you richer rather than merely entertained.

I notice that when people are truly engaged — truly present — they have a quality about them that is almost impossible to fake. Their eyes change. Their breathing slows. There is a particular stillness, a kind of luminous calm, that attends the moment when someone stops looking at the next thing and simply sees the thing in front of them. It might be a tree in winter, stripped of leaves and standing like a skeleton against a white sky. It might be a child's face, mid-thought, the expression shifting from puzzlement to wonder. It might be a page of text that suddenly opens like a door.

These moments are not rare because the world is lacking. The world is perpetually overflowing with astonishing things. The stars alone — a hundred billion in our galaxy, and our galaxy one of trillions — should be enough to stop every conversation on earth. The fact that we carry entire universes inside our skulls, that neurons are firing in patterns so complex we cannot begin to map them, that consciousness itself exists at all and can turn to contemplate its own existence — this is not a small thing. This is the most improbable and glorious thing that has ever happened in the known universe.

And yet we spend our days refreshing screens.

I don't say this with judgment. I include myself entirely in this critique. I am not above distraction. But I think there is something worth naming here, which is the quiet tragedy of a life spent in shallow water. You can spend an entire lifetime skimming the surface of experience and never once plunge beneath it. You can read a thousand books and understand none of them. You can attend a thousand conversations and hear no one. You can eat ten thousand meals and taste nothing.

Or you can do the opposite. You can decide that your attention is not an infinite resource but a sacred one. You can decide that the quality of your presence matters more than the quantity of your consumption. You can let a single moment expand to fill the whole sky.

I think this is what it means to be fully alive — not to have seen everything, but to have truly seen one thing. Not to have done everything, but to have truly done one thing with the full weight of your being. Not to have loved everyone, but to have truly loved someone or something with a gaze so steady and so generous that the object of that love could not help but glow.

It's such a simple idea. Stay with what is in front of you. Let it be enough. Let it transform you.

And then do it again tomorrow.
